clips.title: How SWE-bench Changed the Way We Test AI Coders
clips.why: SWE-bench is the public version of what we build: real issues from real repos, graded by the tests of the real fix. This short part explains what it measures and why a cleaned-up Verified subset exists.
look: Each task pairs an issue with the repo at the moment before the fix, which is our base commit.
The grade comes from the tests of the fix that was really merged, our hidden tests.
Why Verified exists: some original tasks were unfair or broken, so people screened them. That is our curation step.
clips.after: TICKET-BENCH is a small, private SWE-bench made from our own merged PRs, with 40 tasks chosen by our own engineers.

clips.title: The End of SWE-Bench Verified — Mia Glaese & Olivia Watkins, OpenAI Frontier Evals
clips.why: The people who built SWE-bench Verified explain how they did it, which is exactly the work our engineers do when they pick 40 tasks.
look: Listen for what the reviewers were asked to judge about each task: is the issue clear, and are the tests fair?
Notice how many tasks did not survive the review. Mining is cheap; good tasks are not.
Think about which of our candidates would fail the same review, for example a ticket whose test checks a detail the ticket never mentions.
clips.after: Our curators ask the same questions, prove each task with the nop and oracle agents, and write down who curated it.

clips.title: The End of SWE-Bench Verified — Mia Glaese & Olivia Watkins, OpenAI Frontier Evals
clips.why: Two ways a bench stops measuring skill: the answers leak into what the model has seen, and tests demand more than the task says. Both are risks for our bench too.
look: Contamination: a model that has seen the fix scores well without solving anything. In the story, Nova saw it through git history.
Unfair tests and narrow specs: a correct fix can fail a test that checks one particular way of doing it.
Ask which of these two a private bench avoids for free, and which it still has to work for.
clips.after: Our repo is private, so public training data is less of a risk, but the checkout, the broker and the task data can still leak, which is why bench mode closes all three.

practice.q: Our product repo squash-merges every PR. For the PR that fixed RH-1102, which commit is the task's base?

options.text: The squash commit of the PR itself
options.why: That commit already contains the fix. An agent starting there has nothing to do, and the nop agent would score 1.

options.text: The parent of the squash commit
options.why: That is main just before the fix landed: the bug is there and the hidden test fails, exactly the moment the ticket describes.
Today's main has the fix and every later change. The task has to start before the fix.

practice.q: Finish the line in mine.py that finds the base commit of a squash-merged PR.
practice.hint: One character that means the parent of a commit in git.
practice.why: merge^ is the commit's first parent. After a squash merge that is main just before the PR landed.

practice.q: Which of these is NOT a way for a past ticket's answer to reach Nova during a bench trial?

options.text: origin/main in a plain clone checked out at the base commit
options.why: It is a leak: origin/main points at today's main, which contains the fix, and git log --all shows it.

options.text: The broker reading the task's source PR when Nova searches for similar changes
options.why: It is a leak, which is why the broker refuses the source PR and anything merged after the base in bench mode.

options.text: The ticket's summary and description up to the merge date
options.why: That is the instruction, the one thing Nova is meant to read. Comments after the merge are left out because they often describe the fix.

practice.q: Finish the rule every task must pass before it joins the bench.
practice.before: Harbor's nop agent must score 0, and the
practice.after: agent, which applies the known fix, must score 1.
practice.hint: The agent that already knows the answer.
practice.why: Scoring both ways proves the hidden tests can tell no work from the real fix. A task that fails either check measures noise.

practice.q: Put the life of a bench task in order.
items: mine.py finds a merged PR with a ticket key, a parent commit and its own tests
convert.py writes the task folder: instruction, hidden tests, base commit and solution
An engineer reads the task, cleans the ticket text and checks that the test is fair
The nop agent scores 0 and the oracle scores 1, so the task is proven
The task joins the 40, and maybe the smoke set of 15
A harness PR triggers a smoke run, and the gate compares its pass@1 with main's
practice.why: Mining is cheap and automatic; people and the two check agents decide which candidates become tasks; only then can a score gate a change.

practice.q: Where should candidates.jsonl and the task folders live?

options.text: In the ai-agents repo, next to the bench code, so they are versioned together
options.why: Agents work on ai-agents. Answers stored there could be read by the agent being scored.

options.text: In the brain's repo, so people can search them
options.why: The brain is indexed and searched by agents too, so the answers would be one search away.

options.text: In a restricted golden-set repo that no agent token covers and the brain never indexes
options.why: The bench code can be public to the team; the answers cannot be anywhere an agent can reach.
